source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC6129392 (author manuscript of Subst Use Misuse 2018;53(6):901-909), read in full in my own browser tab, including the reference list; Figure 1 (redrawn from Piazza et al., 1989) is an image whose values were not needed for the claim's numbers, which are all in the running text

claims.overstatement: Two framing points. (1) 'The 1989 study that named telescoping': Marks & Clark say Lisansky first used 'telescoped development' in 1958, citing the 1952 WHO report, and that Piazza et al. are widely credited with defining the term in 1989. Better: 'the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term'. (2) The opening says the faster course was described in treatment and self-help samples. But the cannabis study Marks & Clark describe (Khan et al., 2013) is, by its title in their reference list, a NESARC analysis, that is, a national general-population survey. The claim calls it only 'a national sample'; it should say that this general-population study is described as finding the faster course for cannabis, second-hand and with its timing measure and adjustment not given.
claims.note: Every Marks number in the statement and magnitude checks against the running text: 1952 WHO report; 98 men, with 15 women's data excluded; 33 women and 105 men; 4.3 years; about 2 and 3 years later first drink and first intoxication; same age at treatment entry; Iowa 3,132 men and 395 women, about 2 vs 3 years after a first attempt to quit; Khan 1,217 women and 3,297 men, 2.5 years; 75 of 103; the term should be discarded. Randall et al. (1999) is listed by Marks & Clark among larger samples with fewer telescoping effects, while Keyes et al. (2010) cite it as clinical evidence of telescoping, so 'described in opposite ways' is right. The paper is a critical history-of-science analysis with no stated search or selection method. The 103/75 citation count comes from a Web of Science and PubMed search with no date or criteria given.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Objectives and Methods; Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: A critical analysis in the history of science: a feminist philosophy of science framework applied to key source publications of the telescoping literature from 1952 onwards. No search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal of studies is described.

anchors.locator: Introduction › History of Telescoping Research › Foundational Background, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Jellinek's stage model came from AA members recalling the ages at which key points of their drinking careers happened. The 36-item questionnaire was designed by AA and mailed through the AA Grapevine, with a 10% response; data were analysed for 98 men. The answers of 15 women were excluded, as too few and too different. The model had 43 symptoms in three stages and was later replicated in over 2,000 participants, all male AA members (Jellinek 1952; WHO 1952).

anchors.locator: Introduction › History of Telescoping Research › Foundational Background, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: In 1952 a WHO Expert Committee on Mental Health (Copenhagen) reported that in women the phases of alcoholism were less clear-cut and development was frequently more rapid. Lisansky cited that report and first used the term 'telescoped development' in 1958.

anchors.locator: Introduction › History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Early evidence came from observational studies in treatment programmes, state hospitals and self-help groups. Mulford (1977) interviewed 3,132 men and 395 women at Iowa community alcoholism service centres, with an interview validated in men: women arrived for treatment about 2 years after their first attempt to quit, men about 3 years after.

anchors.locator: Introduction › History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Piazza et al. (1989), widely credited with defining telescoping: 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups gave their ages at first drink, first drunk, first alcohol-related problem and first treatment admission. Women and men entered treatment at the same age, but women started drinking 2 years later and were first intoxicated 3 years later. The mean interval from first problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter in women, who also accumulated the same number of symptoms in less time.

anchors.locator: Introduction › History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 6th paragraph; References (Khan et al., 2013)
anchors.extracted: Khan et al. (2013) are described as finding the time from first cannabis use to onset of cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, in a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men; the timing measure and any adjustment are not described. The reference title shows a NESARC analysis, that is, a general-population survey. Larger and more diverse samples are said to give discrepant results, with fewer telescoping effects (Johnson 2005; Keyes 2008; Randall 1999; Slutske 2015; Wagner & Anthony 2007). Keyes et al. (2010) concluded telescoping is not seen in the general population and may occur only in people who reach a clinical diagnosis; the mechanism has not been demonstrated.

anchors.locator: Introduction › History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 7th paragraph
anchors.extracted: A Web of Science and PubMed search found 103 peer-reviewed articles citing Piazza et al. (1989). Of these, 75 did not study telescoping directly but cited it as rationale or context for sex and gender differences. No search date or criteria are given.

anchors.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Conclusions › Feminist Philosophy as a Transformative Framework for Future Directions, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: The authors contend that the term perpetuates a biased, male-referenced framework and should be discarded. They describe the research on sex differences in progression as limited and discrepant, and say the term outgrew it to become a general narrative of sex and gender differences.

anchors.locator: Introduction › Bias in Telescoping Research, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The stage model rests on a convenience sample of mostly male, active AA members and should not be generalized to problem drinkers at large, still less to women. The progressive-disease premise ignores people who remit without formal treatment or return to non-problem drinking (selection bias).

After 1989, telescoping was reported for drugs: women using opiates and cannabis were said to develop problems faster and enter treatment sooner than men (Hernandez-Avila 2004; Khan 2013; Lewis 2014). Opiates are not split by type, and no heroin exception is mentioned.

anchors.locator: Introduction › History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 9th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Social explanations are offered for quicker treatment entry in women: harsher social disapproval, and family or authorities stepping in when children are thought to be at risk. Causal links between these factors and telescoping have not been demonstrated.

key_findings.correction: Change 'who named telescoping' to 'widely credited with defining the term telescoping'. The paper says Lisansky first used 'telescoped development' in 1958 (key finding 1), so the 1989 paper did not coin the idea. All numbers confirmed: 33 women and 105 men; first drink about 2 and first intoxication about 3 years later; same age at treatment entry; 4.3 years.
Add that the reference list title shows Khan et al. (2013) is a NESARC analysis, a general-population survey; the text says only that participants were recruited nationally.

reporting_issues.note: The Rousanville misspelling is also in the Introduction, 1st paragraph.
Piazza et al. (1986) also used 18 Jellinek symptoms (Empirical Research, 4th paragraph).
This is a discrepancy between two papers, not within this one; checked against Keyes et al. (2010), Introduction, 1st paragraph (refs 3–6).

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; high overall follows from the high search domain.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the conclusions are normative and presented as such.

missed: Khan et al. (2013), described as a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men, is a NESARC analysis by its reference title, so it is a general-population study reported second-hand as finding the time to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women. The card's results_show and where_it_stands present the general-population evidence as negative (Keyes et al., 2010) and should add this study, with its timing measure and adjustment unknown.
